plan.contextChunk: This figure is a potential energy curve for a pair of hydrogen atoms, drawn on a pale blue field with small green spheres added to show the atomic arrangement at three points along it. A tall gradient arrow at the far left, shaded from cream to orange and labeled Energy, gives the sense of the vertical scale, while the plot's own vertical axis is marked only with a plus sign, a 0, and a minus sign, with a horizontal dashed line drawn across at zero. The horizontal axis is labeled Internuclear distance and ends in a magenta arrow pointing right. One magenta curve drops steeply from the upper left, crosses below zero, reaches a rounded minimum, then rises gradually and levels off toward the zero line at large separation. At the top of the steep branch two green spheres overlap, annotated HH (too close). At the right, two widely separated spheres sit above a magenta dashed line joining the letters H and H, annotated H - - - H (too far). At the bottom of the well two just-touching spheres are labeled H-H, and a short vertical dashed line drops from the minimum to the axis, tagged 74 pm, with a green arrow labeled Bond length pointing to it. The depth and position of the single minimum, read against the two extremes flanking it, mark the separation at which attraction and nuclear repulsion balance and fix the length of a covalent bond.

interactionPlan.concept: The H-H bond length (74 pm) is the internuclear distance at the minimum of the potential-energy curve, the single point where electron-nucleus attraction and nucleus-nucleus repulsion exactly balance; moving the atoms either closer or farther apart raises the energy.
elements: vertical gradient arrow at far left, shaded cream (bottom) to orange (top), labeled 'Energy'
y-axis with three tick labels: '+', '0', '−'
horizontal dashed line across the plot at energy = 0
x-axis labeled 'Internuclear distance' ending in a rightward magenta arrow
magenta potential-energy curve: steep repulsive wall at small distance, rounded minimum, gradual rise leveling toward the zero line at large distance
atom-pair sketch at top-left: two overlapping green spheres, labeled 'HH (too close)'
atom-pair sketch at the well minimum: two just-touching green spheres, labeled 'H—H'
atom-pair sketch at right: two widely separated green spheres above a magenta dashed line, labeled 'H - - - H (too far)'
short vertical dashed line dropping from the curve minimum to the x-axis, tagged '74 pm'
green arrow labeled 'Bond length' pointing to the 74 pm dashed line
movable marker dot on the magenta curve (driven by the slider) with a faint vertical guide to the x-axis

interactions.label: Internuclear distance (pm)
interactions.teaches: Dragging the separation moves a point along the energy curve: energy climbs steeply when atoms are forced too close (repulsion dominates), sits at the minimum at 74 pm (balanced), and rises back toward zero as they pull apart (attraction fades) — so the bond length is the distance of lowest energy

Clicking the repulsive wall, the energy well, or the far-separated tail highlights the matching atom sketch, making explicit why energy is high when nuclei overlap, lowest at bonding distance, and near zero when the atoms no longer interact

demo_steps.title: Too close: repulsion wins
demo_steps.narration: At very short separation the marker sits high on the steep left wall and the two green spheres overlap — the positively charged nuclei repel each other, so the energy is large and positive.

demo_steps.title: Bond length: the energy minimum
demo_steps.narration: At 74 pm the marker rests at the bottom of the well where the spheres just touch; here electron-nucleus attraction and nucleus-nucleus repulsion balance, giving the most stable (lowest-energy) arrangement — the H-H bond length.

demo_steps.title: Too far: no interaction
demo_steps.narration: Pulling the atoms apart moves the marker up the gentle right branch toward the dashed zero line as the spheres separate; with no overlap the atoms stop attracting each other and the energy approaches that of two isolated H atoms.

interactionPlan.keyInsight: A covalent bond forms at the internuclear distance where the potential energy is minimized — the exact point where attractive and repulsive forces cancel — and any deviation from that distance costs energy.
interactionPlan.reconstructionNotes: Pale blue plot background. Draw one smooth magenta curve: a near-vertical repulsive wall on the left, a rounded minimum roughly a third of the way across, then a long gentle asymptote approaching the horizontal dashed zero line from below on the right. Place the three green-sphere sketches above their corresponding curve regions (overlapping pair top-left, touching pair at the minimum, separated pair at right with a magenta dashed connector). Left margin: a tall vertical arrow filled with a cream-to-orange gradient and the word 'Energy' rotated along it. Y-axis shows only '+', '0', '−' with the dashed line at 0. X-axis label 'Internuclear distance' with a magenta arrowhead. From the minimum drop a short vertical dashed line to the axis tagged '74 pm', and add a green horizontal arrow labeled 'Bond length' pointing at it. Tie a filled marker dot to the slider so it rides the curve and a faint vertical guide tracks the x-axis; on click of a region, emphasize that region's curve segment and brighten its atom sketch while dimming the others.

authoredContext:
How close are the two nuclei in the H2 molecule? If they are too close, they will repel each other because both are positively charged. Yet if they’re too far apart, they won’t be able to share the bonding electrons. Thus, there is an optimum distance between nuclei that leads to maximum stability (the figure). Called the bond length, this distance is 74 pm in the H–H molecule. Every covalent bond has both a characteristic bond strength and bond length.

A plot of energy versus internuclear distance for two hydrogen atoms. The distance between nuclei at the minimum energy point is the bond length.

A graph of energy versus internuclear distance. A horizontal line separates the positive and negative energy and a curve with a single trough at 74 ppm is shown.

discrepancies: An extra magenta marker dot sits at the curve minimum (the slider-driven indicator); the source has no such dot, only the dashed vertical line and '74 pm' tag
The top-left 'HH (too close)' pair is drawn as two lightly overlapping circles, whereas the source shows a near-merged pair with a vertical seam (heavier overlap)
The source curve's right branch levels off and terminates near the 'too far' annotation, while the generated curve continues to the right plot edge asymptoting to zero
The '74 pm' label is right-aligned just left of the dashed line rather than centered directly beneath it as in the source
evaluation.notes: The Morse-potential curve, pale-blue panel, gradient Energy arrow, three green sphere-pair annotations, dashed zero line, 74 pm tag and green Bond-length arrow all match the source faithfully, and the slider/click/step-player interactions are functional and conceptually correct; the main weaknesses are the added abstract marker dot (the real H-spheres do not animate with the slider) and small label-placement/styling deviations from the original.
action_items: Drive the actual green H-sphere pair (overlap at short r, touching at 74 pm, separated with dashed bond at large r) from the slider value instead of only moving a plain magenta dot, so the interaction visually demonstrates the same three regimes the static annotations depict
Center the '74 pm' label directly beneath the dashed vertical minimum line to match the source layout
Render the top-left 'too close' pair with stronger overlap (nearly merged circles with a thin vertical seam) to match the source depiction
